summary: SEC Insights makes every LLM call through LlamaIndex's OpenAI chat LLM, so the migration is two client constructions: the shared Settings.llm behind sub-question generation, the per-document retrieval engines, the qa/refine synthesiser and (via a model_copy) the per-document quantitative agent; and the streaming, tool-calling OpenAIAgent the chat UI talks to. Both now take the vendored runtime as their httpx client, which translates their Chat Completions traffic to Router's /v1/responses when RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set and goes to OpenAI untouched when it is not. Pointing the clients straight at Router was not an option: this code calls Chat Completions, for which Router has no endpoint. Embeddings stay on OpenAI, because Router serves no embeddings endpoint. Doing this surfaced one real break that no test would have caught: the runtime opened every translated stream with a chunk carrying content "", and LlamaIndex skips a leading chunk only when its content is None, so the chunk was yielded as a real delta with no tool_calls, OpenAIAgentWorker latched is_function False on it, and the app's top-level chat returned an empty answer and never called its tools. I reproduced that against a local OpenAI-shaped server with no Router involved, fixed the runtime to send content None (what OpenAI itself sends on tool-call streams), and verified the whole chain on the real Router: 15 of 15 requests at 200, tools called, correct answers, off-topic questions still refused. The existing tests are unchanged and pass at the baseline counts.
reviewed: I read every LLM call this app makes and costed the shape of a chat turn by stage, measuring 12 retrieval requests to 3 chat requests for one document and two questions on the real Router. That ratio drives the top proposal (split the retrieval model from the chat model, which one env var currently ties together) and the two availability items (cross-vendor fallbacks, and pinning the standard tier before anyone picks a Flex-eligible model). I checked each Router lever against this app rather than in the abstract: Flex is wrong here because every call has a user waiting on a stream; prompt caching only pays once a conversation's prefix passes about 1,024 tokens, so it is proposed with that caveat rather than built; shadow models and Switchyard need an account strategy a human switches on and are not listed as code changes. I also looked past Router at what the spend buys, which turned up a per-document quantitative agent whose tool takes no arguments (so its tool-call round trip carries no information) and an embedding model the app silently never selected. Three items are built and tested on branches; five are proposed, because each needs either a quality judgement on a different model or a data migration.

calls.task: sub-question generation, per-document retrieval, qa/refine synthesis

items.title: Route both LlamaIndex OpenAI chat clients through Router
items.summary: The two OpenAI chat LLMs this app builds take the vendored runtime as their httpx client, so all of its chat traffic is translated to Router's /v1/responses.
items.gains: One gateway and one key for every LLM call the app makes, with per-request spend, the serving provider and usage.cost recorded per request; model and vendor become a configuration change rather than an SDK change; router.policy.json can add Router-only fields without touching the code.
items.price: no change: gpt-4o-mini at $0.15/$0.60 per 1M is the same list price through Router, and usage.cost matched list price exactly in the fact sheet's measurements.
items.why: Every LLM call in this app comes from a LlamaIndex OpenAI LLM, and there are only two constructions of one: llama_index_settings.py:28 sets Settings.llm, which drives sub-question generation, the per-document retrieval query engines and the qa/refine synthesiser, and is deep-copied at chat/tools.py:152 for the per-document quantitative agent; engine.py:287 builds the streaming, tool-calling agent the user talks to. Wrapping those two constructions therefore routes everything, including the site the scanner cannot see. The runtime, rather than pointing the clients at Router directly, because LlamaIndex calls Chat Completions and Router has no /v1/chat/completions endpoint - a native base-URL swap would 404 on every request. The runtime also keeps the app on OpenAI, byte for byte, until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off again, so this is reversible without a deploy.

evidence.detail: The repo's test command, unchanged: 8 passed (import + settings + get_api_query_engine_tool + get_chat_engine smoke) and 7 passed (pytest tests/), the same counts as the base commit.

The app's own chain (index_to_query_engine, get_custom_response_synth, SubQuestionQueryEngine, and the top-level OpenAIAgent driven exactly as app/chat/messaging.py drives it) against the real Router: 15 of 15 requests 200 on /v1/responses, provider=openai. Retrieval answered '$383,285 million' from the filing, the streaming agent called its tool and returned a 532-589 character answer across runs, and an off-topic question was still refused per SYSTEM_MESSAGE.

router-migrate check --run against router-sim: 4 of 4 requests valid on /v1/responses, each attributed to its client construction. Only api.openai.com embedding traffic was blocked, which is the traffic that stays on the provider by design.

router-migrate check --all: 2 of 2 call sites the scanner sees ROUTE. chat/tools.py:152 is invisible to the scanner but routes, because it copies the wrapped Settings.llm - confirmed in the simulator, where its request is attributed to client=app/llama_index_settings.py:_setup_llama_index_settings.

items.title: Runtime: content null on the first streamed chunk
items.summary: The runtime opened every translated stream with a chunk carrying content "", which made LlamaIndex treat a tool-call stream as a text answer and drop the tool calls.
items.gains: The app's top-level streaming chat calls its tools and answers; without this it returns an empty response to every message.
items.why: The runtime's stream writer emits a role-priming chunk before the first text or tool-call event. It carried content "". LlamaIndex's OpenAI._astream_chat skips a leading chunk only when both its content and its tool_calls are None - a guard written for exactly this case - so a chunk with content "" was yielded as a real delta with no tool_calls. OpenAIAgentWorker's is_function then latched False on that first chunk, set is_function_false_event, and streamed the turn as a text answer: no tool call, and an empty response that app/chat/messaging.py would show as 'Sorry, I either wasn't able to understand your question'. Since every answer in this app comes from a tool, that is total failure of the user-facing path, and no existing test calls an LLM so nothing would have caught it. OpenAI itself sends content null on tool-call streams, so None is both the fix and the faithful shape. Separate commit from m1 because it edits the vendored runtime, which the outside check flags for review - but note m1 is broken without it.

evidence.detail: Same prompt, same model (gpt-4o-mini) on the real Router. Before: astream_chat gave tool_calls=[], 1 chunk, answer ''. After: tool_calls=['Apple'], 8 chunks, the full answer. achat (non-streaming) was correct both times, which is why only the streamed path was affected.

Reproduced with no Router involved, against a local server emitting OpenAI's own chunk shapes: with OpenAI's sequence the app's agent returned tool_calls=1 and a 302-character answer; inserting a single leading chunk with content "" ahead of it gave tool_calls=0, 1 chunk, answer '' - the exact pre-fix Router symptom.

items.title: Embeddings stay on OpenAI
items.summary: Settings.embed_model keeps calling OpenAI directly, because Router serves no embeddings endpoint.
items.why: /v1/embeddings returns a plain-text 404 on Router, and embeddings are not in its endpoint list, so there is nothing to route to. The runtime would keep this traffic on the provider even if the client were wrapped, so the client is left alone rather than given a transport that can only pass it through. The practical consequence is that the OpenAI key must stay configured after the migration - see n1.

evidence.detail: In the offline simulator run the only blocked host was api.openai.com, from the embedding call - confirming embeddings never attempt Router. Against the real Router the same call reached OpenAI and returned 401 for the dummy key used in testing, which is the provider path behaving as intended.

items.title: The OpenAI key must stay configured
items.summary: Two paths still need OPENAI_API_KEY after the migration: embeddings, and the runtime's provider retry when Router refuses a request before generating.
items.why: Embeddings never go to Router (m3). Separately, when Router refuses before generating - 403, 404 model_not_found, an unknown or unsupported parameter, an invalid value, 501 - the runtime sends the original request to OpenAI once, so the app survives a Router-side configuration problem. That path needs the provider key; ROUTER_MIGRATE_FALLBACK=0 turns it off if you would rather see Router's errors. Removing OPENAI_API_KEY would break retrieval (no embeddings) even though chat would keep working. ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 is the kill switch that returns everything to OpenAI without a code change.

evidence.detail: app/core/config.py requires OPENAI_API_KEY at import time (it is a required field on PreviewPrefixedSettings and is also exported into os.environ), so the app will not start without it regardless.

items.title: Split the retrieval model from the chat model
items.summary: One env var sets both the user-facing chat model and the retrieval fan-out behind it; splitting them lets the 80% of requests nobody reads run on a cheaper model.
items.gains: Measured on the real Router, one document and two questions produced 12 retrieval requests to 3 chat requests, and the retrieval ones carry the large payloads (3 retrieved chunks of about 512 tokens each, per sub-question, per document, plus refine passes). Those calls are mechanical: generate sub-questions, extract an answer from supplied context, refine. Moving only them to gpt-5-mini ($0.25/$2.00 per 1M, cache-read $0.025) or gpt-5-nano ($0.05/$0.40) from gpt-4o-mini ($0.15/$0.60) cuts the dominant input cost by 3x at nano, while the answer the user actually reads keeps - or improves on - its current model. It also makes the two tunable independently, which is the only way to spend more on the answer and less on the plumbing.
items.loses: A different model gives different answers, and nothing offline measures quality: sub-question decomposition over financial filings is the part most likely to degrade on a smaller model, and a bad decomposition silently produces a confident wrong answer. gpt-5-nano is also a reasoning model, so its output tokens include reasoning and its latency is less predictable than gpt-4o-mini's. This needs a human to compare answers on real filings before it ships, which is why it is proposed rather than built.
items.why: settings.OPENAI_CHAT_LLM_NAME is read at both llama_index_settings.py:28 and engine.py:287, so today the two roles cannot diverge - and the roles could not be less alike. The chat model routes tools and writes the prose a financial analyst reads; the retrieval model summarises chunks it was handed. Router is what makes this cheap to act on: both models are catalog ids on the same surface, so the change is a second setting plus a second model name, with no SDK or vendor work. The temperature these clients set (0 at engine.py:287, LlamaIndex's 0.1 default on Settings.llm) is not an obstacle even though Router returns 400 for temperature on reasoning models including gpt-5-nano: the runtime drops temperature and top_p when it translates a request for a model whose catalog entry refuses them. Land it with i4: gpt-5-mini and gpt-5-nano are Flex-eligible and Router's account default is cost-efficient routing, so without the standard-tier pin this change would quietly expose user-waiting requests to Flex queueing, measured at up to 61 s on gpt-5-nano. i2 is what lets you verify the split and watch the two stages' spend separately afterwards.

items.title: Fail over to another vendor when OpenAI is unavailable
items.summary: Add a ranked fallback list per stage in router.policy.json so a provider outage or rate limit degrades answers instead of killing chat.
items.gains: Today OpenAI is a single point of failure for the entire product: a 429 or 5xx from the provider ends the chat turn, and the runtime deliberately passes timeouts, 429s and 5xxs back to the app rather than retrying. A models list on /v1/responses lets Router try the next candidate within the same request, across vendors - so sec-retrieval can fall through to claude-haiku-5-5 ($0.10/$0.50) or gpt-4.1-mini, and sec-chat to a candidate that supports tools. For a product whose whole value is answering questions about filings, answering from a different vendor beats not answering.
items.loses: A different model answers those requests, and the response does not say which candidate failed, so an outage shows up as a quiet change in answer style rather than an incident. The least capable candidate caps tools, structured output and context for the whole request, so sec-chat's candidates must all support tool calling. Fallbacks and Flex do not combine (allow_flex_tier is ignored with a list), and the docs say there is no fallback once a stream has started - so for the streamed chat turn this covers failures before the first token, not mid-stream ones. Per the fact sheet, truncated attempts are still billed.
items.why: This is declarative - a fallbacks key per feature in router.policy.json, no application code - but it genuinely changes which model answers a financial question, so it is a decision rather than a default. It wants i2 first: sec-chat and sec-retrieval need different candidate lists, because only the chat stage sends tools, and per-stage policy keys are exactly what the labels provide. The fact sheet marks fallback behaviour on real provider outages as documented but not measured, so this should ship with a deliberate test against a model id the key cannot use, which is a known fall-through case.

items.title: Label each LLM stage for Router's spend views
items.summary: Each LLM client names its stage in the x-router-migrate-feature header, so Router can separate the answer the user reads from the retrieval fan-out behind it.
items.gains: Without this, every request from a chat turn is labelled with the first application frame on the stack - app/chat/messaging.py:handle_chat_message for all of them - so Router's per-request spend and latency views cannot tell the two stages apart, and router.policy.json has no stable key to target either one. With it, the split is visible (12 sec-retrieval to 3 sec-chat, measured) and policy can be written per stage, which i1 and i3 both need. The labels also become metadata.feature on Router, so spend attribution survives in Ramp's own views.
items.loses: The label strings become deployment configuration: renaming one silently drops its router.policy.json entry, since an unmatched feature just falls through to defaults. The per-document quantitative agent cannot get its own label this way - app/chat/tools.py:152 deep-copies the shared LLM and the copy carries the parent's already-built SDK client, so headers set on the copy never reach the wire (measured) - so it inherits sec-retrieval until i5 gives it a fresh client.
items.why: Everything else on this list is a cost or availability decision, and none of them can be judged without knowing where the money goes. This is the cheapest possible way to find out: two default_headers arguments and two constants, no behaviour change at all. It is built because it is risk-free and because the ratio it exposes is the evidence for i1.

items.title: Drop the quantitative agent's empty tool-call round trip
items.summary: The per-document quantitative agent spends an LLM round trip deciding to call a tool that takes no arguments and always returns the same data.
items.gains: Removes one LLM call per document per quantitative sub-question. app/chat/tools.py builds a whole OpenAIAgent per document whose only tool is extract_data_from_sec_document, and that function signature is (*args, **kwargs) - it ignores every argument and always fetches the same polygon.io financials for its document. So the agent's first call carries no information: it can only decide 'yes, fetch'. describe_financials already returns finished English sentences, so the data needs no interpretation to be readable. Fetching deterministically and answering in one call halves the LLM calls on the quantitative path and removes a failure mode (the agent declining to call its tool). It is also the natural moment to give this stage its own Router label, which i2 cannot (see its loses).
items.loses: The agent currently decides whether to fetch at all and can retry or reframe; a deterministic fetch always calls polygon.io, so a question that needed no financials still pays an API call, and polygon.io failures become unconditional rather than something the agent can route around. The tool's exception handler returns 'No answer found.', which an agent can interpret and a single-call engine would hand straight to the synthesiser. Changing the engine's shape also changes which CBEventType events reach the UI's sub-process timeline, which users see.
items.why: This is the fact sheet's own point - Router makes model calls cheap to change, which also makes it cheap to see which calls should not be model calls at all. Here the evidence is unusually clean: the tool cannot use arguments, so the round trip that produces them is pure cost and latency on a path where a user is waiting. It is a rework rather than a change because it replaces an agent with a query engine and alters the events the frontend renders, so it needs a product decision, not just a config switch.

items.title: Pin the standard tier: nothing here runs unattended
items.summary: router.policy.json sends service_tier "default" on every request, so a Flex-eligible model can never queue a request a user is waiting on.
items.gains: Closes a trapdoor at no cost. Router's account default is cost-efficient routing, so a Flex-eligible model is served at Flex without opting in, and a Flex call has been measured at 61 s on gpt-5-nano. Every LLM call this app makes happens while a user watches a streamed answer, so none of them should ever queue. The same policy adds metadata.product for Ramp spend management.
items.loses: Gives up the Flex discount, measured at exactly -50% on gpt-5.4-mini - which is the right trade here, since there is no unattended work to spend it on, but it does mean a future background job in this codebase would need its own policy entry to opt back in.
items.why: gpt-4o-mini has no Flex tier, so today this changes nothing - that is precisely why it is worth landing now rather than later. The moment OPENAI_CHAT_LLM_NAME points at any of the 17 Flex-eligible OpenAI ids, which is exactly what i1 proposes, user-waiting traffic silently becomes eligible for queueing with no code change and no signal. The policy uses defaults rather than per-feature entries so it holds whatever the labels are, with or without i2.

items.title: Runtime: read the Router stream to EOF
items.summary: The stream writer abandoned the Router response at [DONE], which made httpcore raise out of the garbage collector on every streamed call.
items.gains: Removes three stderr tracebacks per chat message from production logs. The writer stopped reading the upstream response as soon as it had emitted data: [DONE], leaving the provider's byte-stream generator suspended mid-read; httpcore's pool stream responds to the GeneratorExit it gets when the collector finalises it by awaiting its own aclose(), which is not allowed there, so each streamed call logged 'async generator ignored GeneratorExit' plus an un-awaited coroutine. Reading to EOF is what the OpenAI SDK does on the direct provider path, which is why the unrouted baseline is clean.
items.loses: The wrapper now waits for the Router response to end rather than returning the moment it has translated the last event. Router's SSE ends right after response.completed so there is nothing to wait for in practice, but it is the same exposure to a provider that holds a connection open that the SDK already takes on the direct path, bounded by the client timeout and provider_timeout rather than by the wrapper.
items.why: Log noise rather than broken behaviour - the response is still closed correctly - but it is noise on this app's main path, three lines per user message, which is enough to bury a real error and enough to make a healthy service look unhealthy. It is separated from the migration so that the migration can be judged on its own: it edits the vendored runtime, which the outside check flags for review.

items.title: Give each conversation its own prompt cache key
items.summary: A per-conversation prompt_cache_key would let multi-turn chats read their repeated system prompt and history from cache instead of paying full input price.
items.gains: Every turn of a conversation resends SYSTEM_MESSAGE plus the whole chat history as the prefix of the request, which is exactly the shape caching pays for. On gpt-4o-mini a cached prefix costs $0.075 instead of $0.15 per 1M; on claude-haiku-5-5 it is $0.01 against $0.10, a 90% cut, so this compounds with i1 if the retrieval stage moves to a Claude model. The fact sheet measured a 9,020-token gpt-4o-mini prompt dropping from $0.00135 to $0.00069 on the second call, and a Claude prompt over Responses dropping 90% once a key was set - Claude does not cache at all without one.
items.loses: Pays nothing on short conversations: caching only applies to an identical prefix above the provider's minimum of about 1,024 tokens, and SYSTEM_MESSAGE is roughly 250, so the first few turns of every conversation are unaffected and the benefit is unmeasured for this app's actual conversation lengths. A per-conversation key also needs application code - router.policy.json can only set prompt_cache_key to $feature, which gives one key for all conversations - so it means threading the conversation id into the request, and prompt_cache_retention is documented but unmeasured.
items.why: Worth doing only after i2 shows what multi-turn traffic actually costs, which is why it is proposed with its caveat rather than built on a guess. The one thing to get right if it ships is prefix order: fixed instructions first, per-request text last, which SYSTEM_MESSAGE plus history already satisfies. Note the runtime already sets prompt_cache_key from the label on Claude requests over Responses, so a Claude retrieval stage would get the coarse version of this for free.

items.title: The app never actually selected its embedding model
items.summary: llama_index_settings.py passes model_type= to OpenAIEmbedding, which takes model=, so the kwarg is silently swallowed and every embedding is text-embedding-ada-002.
items.gains: The code imports OpenAIEmbeddingModelType.TEXT_EMBED_3_SMALL and clearly intends to use it, but OpenAIEmbedding's parameter is model, not model_type, so the value lands in **kwargs and the default stands. Measured: the constructed object reports model_name text-embedding-ada-002; passing model= instead reports text-embedding-3-small. ada-002 is a 2022 model at $0.10 per 1M against $0.02 for 3-small - five times the price for weaker retrieval. Retrieval quality is what every expensive LLM call downstream is summarising, so this is the cheapest available improvement to answer quality, and it reduces embedding spend at the same time.
items.loses: Not a free switch: the vectors already in pg_vector are ada-002, and the two models' embeddings are not comparable, so changing it without re-embedding would degrade retrieval rather than improve it. It needs a backfill - re-running the seed over the corpus and swapping the vector table - with a window where queries and stored vectors disagree. Both models are 1536-dimensional, so nothing will crash to warn you; the failure mode is silently worse answers.
items.why: Not a Router change, and I am flagging it rather than fixing it for that reason. It belongs on this list because it is the same question Router forces you to ask about every model call - is this call actually configured the way you think - and here the answer is no, in the one place where a mistake degrades every answer the product gives. The fix in the code is one word; the work is the data migration, which is why it is a rework.
